text: Karl Ludwig, Count of Ficquelmont (German: [ˈfɪkɛlˌmɔnt]; French: Charles-Louis comte de Ficquelmont; 23 March 1777 – 7 April 1857), was an Austrian aristocrat, statesman, and General of the cavalry of the Austrian Imperial army of French noble origin. Born Gabriel-Charles-Louis-Bonnaventure, Count de Ficquelmont, at the Castle of Dieuze in the present-day French département of Moselle, he belonged to a noble family from Lorraine dating back to the 14th century (House of Ficquelmont) and was introduced to King Louis XVI at Versailles in 1789. Shortly after, the French Revolution began, and as aristocrats, his family was targeted; several relatives were beheaded and many estates were confiscated during the Terreur era. Ficquelmont joined the "Army of the Princes" to fight against revolutionary France. He entered the military service of the Habsburg monarchy in 1793 and participated in all Austrian campaigns during the Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars, earning a reputation as a brilliant military officer. In 1809, he rose to the rank of Oberst and was appointed chief of staff to Archduke Ferdinand Karl Joseph of Austria-Este. In 1811 and 1812, he led troops in Spain, where his victories drew the attention of Emperor Napoleon I, who unsuccessfully attempted to recruit him. He was elevated to the rank of Generalmajor in 1814 and received the capitulation of Lyon a few months later. Over the following decades, Ficquelmont advanced in the Austrian military, achieving various promotions. In 1815, due to his status as a skilled and loyal military officer, he was approached to represent Austria as a diplomat. After the War of the Sixth Coalition ended, he was sent to Stockholm as Austrian Ambassador Extraordinary to Sweden to smooth relations with the newly elected Swedish heir, Bernadotte, ensuring his inclusion in the coalition leading to the Congress of Vienna—mission successfully completed and marking the start of his diplomatic career. Following Napoleon’s fall, Italy became a key sphere of influence for the Austrian Empire, and in 1820, Ficquelmont was appointed Ambassador to Tuscany and Lucca to strengthen Austrian influence over Grand Duke Ferdinand III of Tuscany. During this time, he met his future wife, Russian countess Dorothea von Tiesenhaussen. In 1821, he was appointed ambassador plenipotentiary to Naples amid the political crisis following the 1820 Carbonari Revolution. A military revolt in Naples in July 1820 forced the king to adopt a constitution modeled on the Spanish Constitution of 1812. The Holy Alliance feared the unrest might spread, prompting Austria to send an army into Naples, which defeated the Neapolitans at Rieti on 7 March 1821 and entered the kingdom. Ficquelmont was sent to manage the subsequent occupation, gaining significant influence over King Ferdinand I and Neapolitan elites and effectively administering domestic and foreign policies. He was recognized as Austria’s key diplomatic asset for his political acumen and social skills, described as possessing Germanic seriousness, Italian subtlety, and the wit of 18th-century French nobility. In 1829, he was appointed Ambassador Extraordinary to Russia. His wife, countess Dorothea von Tiesenhausen, was the granddaughter of Prince Kutuzov and a member of the prominent Tiesenhausen family, becoming influential in the politics of Emperor Nicholas I. The Saltykov Mansion, the Austrian Embassy, was described as a "place of wisdom and intelligence" and as "(...) the setting of the two most illustrious salons of the period (1830s), reigned over by Ficquelmont's wife." Ficquelmont and Dorothea's influence in Russia was long-lasting, and as a sign of appreciation, Emperor Nicholas I awarded him the Orders of St. Andrew, St. Alexander Nevsky, St. Vladimir, and St. Anna. In 1839, Ficquelmont was recalled to Vienna to serve in the Foreign Office during Prince Metternich’s absence. In 1840, he was appointed Minister of the State and Conferences and chief of staff of the Imperial Army, becoming not only Metternich’s right-hand man but officially the second most senior statesman in the Empire, with the observation that "Count de Ficquelmont stands just behind or next to Prince Metternich (..) Every conference starts with Count de Ficquelmont and ends with Prince Metternich." In Vienna, the Ficquelmonts were among the most prominent social figures, with Ficquelmont’s salon being described as the most sophisticated, erudite, mindful, and beloved in the city. In 1841, his daughter, countess Elizabeth Alexandrine, married Prince Edmund von Clary-und-Aldringen, heir to one of the Empire’s most prominent princely families. In 1847, Ficquelmont was sent to Milan as acting Chancellor of Lombardy–Venetia and senior advisor to Archduke Rainer Joseph of Austria to restore Austrian rule amid growing resentment. After only a few months, he was recalled to Vienna to lead the Council of War as the Revolutions of 1848 began. From early 1848 to 13 March, he led the Austrian Council of War. On 13 March, Prince Metternich resigned and fled; Ficquelmont then assumed duties until 17 March, when Count Franz Anton von Kolowrat was appointed Minister-President. From 17 March until the fall of the Kolowrat cabinet on 3 April, Ficquelmont managed the Department of Foreign Affairs and the War Ministry. On 4 April, he became Minister-President of the Empire, but due to his close ties with the Metternich System and the Russian tsar, popular opposition forced him to resign on 4 May. The period was violent: his wife, Countess Dolly, was arrested twice by the Venetian guarda civil and eventually fled Venice on an English ship with her daughter, son-in-law, and grandchildren. Additionally, his kinsman in the War Ministry, Count Theodor Franz Baillet von Latour, was lynched during the Vienna Uprising of October 1848. After the revolutions ended, Ficquelmont refused to return to politics and dedicated himself to writing and publishing political essays that gained wide recognition across Europe. In 1852, Emperor Franz Joseph I of Austria made him a Knight of the Golden Fleece, the most prestigious order of the Empire. In his later years, he retired first to his palace in Vienna and later to his Venetian palace, where he died in 1857 at the age of 81. As a result of the French Revolution, the Ficquelmont family dispersed across Europe, with members settling in Italy, Hungary, England, and the Netherlands. One of Charles-Louis’s uncles, Count Antoine-Charles de Ficquelmont (1753–1833), recreated the title Count de Ficquelmont in the Dutch nobility on 16 July 1822. Charles-Louis had five siblings, of whom only one had children—a girl and a boy. His niece, Clotilde de Vaux (Paris 1815–Paris 1846), inspired philosopher Auguste Comte’s Religion of Humanity, organized around public veneration of Humanity through a Goddess modeled after her. In 1821, at age 44, Ficquelmont married countess Dorothea von Tiesenhausen (St. Petersburg 1804 – Venice 1863), 17, granddaughter of Prince Kutuzov. Countess Dorothea was renowned for her beauty; a famous Neapolitan proverb praised her as « Vedi Napoli, la Ficquelmont e poi muori » (« To see Naples, the countess Ficquelmont, and die »). She was also known for her letter-writing and diary, which were published in Italian and Russian in 1950, documenting her life as a high society aristocrat in 19th-century Europe. The couple had one daughter, Elisabeth-Alexandrine-Marie-Thérèse de Ficquelmont (Naples 1825 – Venice 1878), Countess de Ficquelmont by birth and Princess Clary und Aldringen by marriage to Edmund, 4th Prince of Clary-Aldringen. Through Elisabeth, he was a grandfather of Prince Siegfried von Clary-Aldringen (Teplitz 1848 – Teplitz 1929) and Count Manfred von Clary-Aldringen (Vienna 1852 – Salzburg 1928).
